content.body: Have you ever wondered how your computer can detect if a linked list has a cycle? Today we'll learn Floyd's Algorithm, a clever way to find cycles using two pointers. You'll implement this efficient solution step by step.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
1. Explain how Floyd's Algorithm detects cycles in linked lists
2. Implement the two-pointer approach in JavaScript
3. Trace through the algorithm step by step
4. Identify when to use this approach vs other methods
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a simple cycle detection problem. Imagine you have a linked list with 3 nodes that forms a cycle. How would you check if there's a cycle?
content.title: Try it
content.prompt: How would you manually check if a 3-node linked list has a cycle?
content.successMessage: Good thinking! You probably imagined following the nodes one by one.

content.body: Now consider a linked list with 5 nodes where the last node points back to the second node. How would you check for a cycle now?
content.title: Try a bigger list
content.prompt: How would you check for a cycle in a 5-node linked list?
content.successMessage: Nice! You're thinking about following the pointers until you either reach the end or find a cycle.

content.body: What about a linked list with 10 nodes where node 7 points back to node 3? How would you detect this cycle?
content.title: One more
content.prompt: How would you detect a cycle in a 10-node linked list?
content.successMessage: Great! You're manually tracing through the list, which is essentially the brute force approach.

content.body: What you just did was manually trace through the linked list - checking each node and following its pointer. This is like the brute force approach where you visit each node and try to detect if you've seen it before.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When the linked list has thousands of nodes, manually tracing or using a simple loop becomes inefficient. We need a smarter method that doesn't require extra memory to track visited nodes. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen - but without actually storing visited nodes! Floyd's Algorithm uses two pointers moving at different speeds. If there's a cycle, the faster pointer will eventually 'lap' the slower one, just like two runners on a circular track.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Imagine two runners on a track. One runs twice as fast as the other. If the track is circular, the faster runner will eventually catch up to the slower one from behind.

content.body: We'll use two pointers: 'slow' moves one step at a time, 'fast' moves two steps at a time. If they ever meet (point to the same node), there's a cycle. If fast reaches the end (null), there's no cycle.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Walkthrough with a 5-node cycle (1→2→3→4→5→2):
Start: slow=1, fast=1
Step 1: slow=2, fast=3
Step 2: slow=3, fast=5
Step 3: slow=4, fast=2
Step 4: slow=5, fast=4
Step 5: slow=2, fast=2 → They meet! Cycle detected.

content.body:
1. Initialize two pointers at the head of the list
2. Move slow pointer one step forward
3. Move fast pointer two steps forward
4. Check if they point to the same node
5. If yes, cycle detected
6. If fast reaches null, no cycle
7. Repeat until conclusion
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called hasCycle that takes a linked list head as parameter. We'll implement Floyd's Algorithm.
steps.hint: Start with the function signature: function hasCycle(head) {}
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named hasCycle that takes head parameter
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set up the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Make sure the function is named hasCycle and takes head as parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create a function called hasCycle(head) {}

steps.title: Initialize pointers
steps.instruction: Inside the function, initialize two pointers: slow and fast, both starting at the head of the list.
steps.hint: Use let slow = head; let fast = head;
steps.expectedOutcome: Two variables slow and fast initialized to head
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Both pointers start at the head of the list.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure both slow and fast are set to head.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember to create two variables: slow and fast, both starting at head.

steps.title: Create the main loop
steps.instruction: Add a while loop that continues as long as fast and fast.next are not null. This ensures we don't try to access null pointers.
steps.expectedOutcome: A while loop checking fast and fast.next
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! The loop will run as long as we can safely move forward.
steps.feedbackPartial: Close! The loop should check both fast and fast.next.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loop condition should be: while (fast && fast.next) {}

steps.title: Move the pointers
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, move slow one step forward and fast two steps forward. Then check if they point to the same node.
steps.hint: slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; then check if (slow === fast)
steps.expectedOutcome: Pointer movement and equality check inside the loop
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You're moving slow one step and fast two steps, then checking if they meet.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost! Make sure to move both pointers and check if they're equal.
steps.feedbackWrong: Inside the loop: move slow one step, fast two steps, then check if they're the same node.

steps.title: Add the final return
steps.instruction: After the loop ends (when fast reaches null), return false to indicate no cycle was found.
steps.hint: Add return false; after the while loop
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've completed Floyd's Algorithm implementation.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost done! Add return false after the while loop.
steps.feedbackWrong: After the loop ends, return false to indicate no cycle.

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented Floyd's Algorithm for cycle detection. Remember: the key insight is using two pointers moving at different speeds. If there's a cycle, they'll eventually meet. This algorithm runs in O(n) time and uses only O(1) extra space, making it very efficient for detecting cycles in linked lists.
